Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This paper considers the propagation of shallow-water solitary and nonlinear periodic waves over a gradual slope with bottom friction in the framework of a variable-coefficient Korteweg-de Vries equation. We use the Whitham averaging method, using a recent development of this theory for perturbed integrable equations. This general approach enables us not only to improve known results on the adiabatic evolution of isolated solitary waves and periodic wave trains in the presence of variable topography and bottom friction, modeled by the Chezy law, but also importantly, to study the effects of these factors on the propagation of undular bores, which are essentially unsteady in the system under consideration. In particular, it is shown that the combined action of variable topography and bottom friction generally imposes certain global restrictions on the undular bore propagation so that the evolution of the leading solitary wave can be substantially different from that of an isolated solitary wave with the same initial amplitude. This non-local effect is due to nonlinear wave interactions within the undular bore and can lead to an additional solitary wave amplitude growth, which cannot be predicted in the framework of the traditional adiabatic approach to the propagation of solitary waves in slowly varying media.

outputs.L1: This paper investigates the propagation of shallow-water solitary waves and nonlinear periodic waves over a gradual slope in the presence of bottom friction, within the framework of a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries equation. We employ the Whitham averaging method, drawing on a recent extension of the theory to perturbed integrable equations. This general approach not only enables us to refine existing results on the adiabatic evolution of isolated solitary waves and periodic wave trains under the influence of variable topography and bottom friction, modeled by the Chezy law, but, importantly, also allows us to examine the effects of these factors on the propagation of undular bores, which are inherently unsteady in the system considered. In particular, we show that the combined effects of variable topography and bottom friction generally impose global constraints on undular bore propagation, such that the evolution of the leading solitary wave may differ substantially from that of an isolated solitary wave with the same initial amplitude. This nonlocal effect arises from nonlinear wave interactions within the undular bore and can result in additional growth of the solitary-wave amplitude that cannot be predicted using the traditional adiabatic approach to solitary-wave propagation in slowly varying media.
outputs.L2: This study examines how shallow-water solitary waves and nonlinear periodic waves travel over a gently varying slope while experiencing bottom friction, using a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries equation. The analysis applies the Whitham averaging method, incorporating a recent extension of the theory to perturbed integrable equations. This framework both refines established results for the adiabatic development of isolated solitary waves and periodic wave trains under changing bathymetry and Chezy-law bottom friction and, crucially, makes it possible to investigate how these influences affect undular bores, whose behavior in the system is inherently unsteady. The results show that the joint effects of nonuniform topography and bottom friction generally place global constraints on undular-bore propagation. Consequently, the leading solitary wave may evolve very differently from an isolated solitary wave having the same initial amplitude. This nonlocal behavior arises from nonlinear interactions among waves within the bore and may produce additional growth in solitary-wave amplitude—an outcome that the conventional adiabatic theory for solitary-wave propagation through slowly varying media cannot predict.
outputs.L3:
The paper investigates the propagation of shallow-water solitary waves and nonlinear periodic wave trains over a gradually varying slope in the presence of bottom friction. The dynamics are modeled using a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries equation, which captures the combined effects of weak nonlinearity, dispersion, changing water depth, and frictional dissipation.

The analysis employs the Whitham averaging method, supplemented by recent developments in the theory of perturbed integrable equations. This framework provides a systematic description of the slow modulation of nonlinear wave parameters, such as amplitude, wavelength, and propagation speed, as the waves encounter variable topography and Chezy-law bottom friction.

The resulting approach refines and extends existing adiabatic theories for both isolated solitary waves and periodic wave trains. In particular, it yields an improved account of how these waves evolve under gradual depth variations and frictional losses. However, the study also shows that the behavior of an undular bore cannot be understood simply by applying isolated-wave theory to its leading solitary wave. Variable topography and bottom friction impose global constraints on the entire modulated wave structure, linking the evolution of the leading edge to the dynamics of the bore as a whole.

Consequently, the leading solitary wave of an undular bore may evolve differently from an isolated solitary wave with the same initial amplitude. Nonlinear interactions among waves within the bore can generate additional growth in the leading-wave amplitude, even when friction acts to dissipate energy. This interaction-driven amplification is absent from traditional adiabatic theory, which treats waves as evolving independently, and highlights the importance of a fully modulated description for predicting undular-bore propagation over variable and frictional environments.
outputs.L4:
The paper develops a modulation-theory description of long, weakly nonlinear shallow-water waves propagating over a slowly varying bottom in the presence of Chezy friction. Starting from a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries equation, it applies Whitham averaging to derive evolution equations for the slowly changing parameters of nonlinear wave trains. This framework is used to study three related regimes: isolated solitary waves, nonlinear periodic waves, and undular bores.

For an isolated solitary wave, the variable depth and bottom friction produce competing effects. Changes in depth modify the balance among nonlinearity, dispersion, and wave speed, while Chezy friction continuously removes energy. Under the usual adiabatic approximation, the wave is assumed to retain a solitary-wave profile whose amplitude and width adjust gradually to local conditions. This provides a useful baseline prediction for the evolution of a single wave over a slope.

The periodic-wave problem is treated by averaging the governing conservation laws over one wavelength. The resulting Whitham equations describe the slow variation of quantities such as the wave amplitude, mean level, wavelength, and phase velocity. Unlike a purely local adiabatic model, these equations retain the nonlinear interactions within the wave train and account for the cumulative influence of variable topography and dissipation.

The same modulation system is then applied to undular bores, which connect two distinct slowly varying flow states through an expanding nonlinear wavetrain. At one edge, the oscillations have small amplitude and are approximately linear; at the other, they approach a sequence of widely separated solitary waves, with the foremost wave forming the leading edge of the bore. Matching conditions at both edges, together with the averaged balance laws, impose global constraints on the entire modulated structure.

These constraints are central to the paper’s conclusions. The leading solitary wave of an undular bore cannot generally be treated as an isolated soliton responding only to the local depth and friction. Its amplitude and speed are coupled to the mean flow, the trailing oscillations, and the evolution of the bore as a whole. Consequently, its behavior may differ substantially from that predicted by conventional adiabatic solitary-wave theory. In particular, nonlinear redistribution within the bore can partly offset frictional decay and may produce greater leading-wave growth during shoaling than an isolated-wave model would predict.

The analysis therefore shows that wave evolution over gradual slopes is governed not only by local shoaling and dissipation but also by the global modulation dynamics of the nonlinear wavetrain. Whitham averaging provides a unified way to describe isolated waves, periodic waves, and undular bores, while clarifying why the leading wave of a bore must be understood as part of a coupled, evolving structure rather than as an independent solitary wave.
outputs.L5: The **Korteweg–de Vries equation**, often abbreviated as the KdV equation, is a mathematical model describing waves in shallow water. It was developed by Dutch mathematicians Diederik Korteweg and Gustav de Vries in the nineteenth century. **This** equation is especially important because it predicts stable solitary waves, known as solitons, which can travel long distances without losing their shape. Today, the Korteweg–de Vries equation is also used in plasma physics, fluid dynamics, and other areas involving nonlinear wave motion.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an academic abstract for a paper on shallow-water solitary waves, periodic waves, and undular bores propagating over a gradual slope with Chezy bottom friction, using a variable-coefficient KdV equation and Whitham averaging theory.
counterfactuals.output: This paper investigates the evolution of shallow-water solitary waves, periodic wavetrains, and undular bores propagating over a gradually varying bottom in the presence of Chézy friction. Under the assumptions of weak nonlinearity, weak dispersion, slow bathymetric variation, and weak dissipation, the governing free-surface equations are reduced to a variable-coefficient Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equation with a nonlinear friction term. Whitham averaging theory is then applied to the associated cnoidal-wave family to derive modulation equations governing the slowly varying wave parameters. The resulting framework describes shoaling, dissipative attenuation, wavelength adjustment, and changes in the leading and trailing edges of undular bores within a unified asymptotic model. Limiting reductions are obtained for isolated solitary waves and small-amplitude periodic waves, yielding evolution laws for wave amplitude, speed, and width over the slope. The analysis shows that bathymetric shoaling and bottom friction act as competing mechanisms: decreasing depth tends to amplify and compress nonlinear waves, whereas Chézy drag removes energy and can suppress amplitude growth and reduce bore extent. Edge relations for undular bores demonstrate how dissipation and topography modify characteristic velocities and wave amplitudes relative to the constant-depth, frictionless KdV theory. These results provide an analytically tractable description of long-wave transformation in coastal and hydraulic settings and clarify the parameter regimes in which topographic amplification, frictional decay, or their balance controls the observed wave evolution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study that applies recent Whitham modulation methods for perturbed integrable equations to analyze nonlinear shallow-water waves over variable topography with friction.
counterfactuals.output:
The study develops a Whitham modulation description of nonlinear, weakly dispersive shallow-water waves propagating over slowly varying bathymetry while experiencing bottom friction. The governing shallow-water model is reduced to a perturbed integrable equation—typically a variable-coefficient or forced KdV equation—whose unperturbed periodic solutions are cnoidal waves parameterized by slowly varying spectral or Riemann variables.

Using modern perturbative Whitham theory, the authors average the perturbations directly over the periodic KdV solution. This yields modulation equations for the local mean flow, wavelength, amplitude, and wave speed, with explicit source terms representing topographic variation and friction. The formulation remains regular in important limits, including small-amplitude waves and isolated solitons, and therefore describes both extended wavetrains and slowly evolving solitary waves.

The analysis shows that variable depth produces shoaling or de-shoaling through changes in amplitude, wavelength, and propagation speed, whereas friction steadily removes wave energy and reduces nonlinear steepening. Their competition can enhance, suppress, or reshape nonlinear wave structures such as cnoidal wavetrains and undular bores. Reduced evolution laws are obtained in harmonic and soliton limits and compared with numerical solutions of the underlying perturbed equation, generally showing good agreement when the bottom and dissipation vary on scales long compared with a wavelength.

The main contribution is a systematic bridge between integrable-wave theory and realistic coastal-wave effects: bathymetry and friction enter as controlled source terms without discarding the nonlinear periodic-wave structure. This provides an efficient alternative to full numerical simulation and clarifies where adiabatic modulation breaks down—for example, near rapidly varying topography, strong dissipation, wave breaking, or modulation singularities.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a journal-style abstract explaining how gradual depth variation and bottom friction affect isolated solitons, periodic wave trains, and the leading solitary wave of an undular bore.
counterfactuals.output: This study examines the combined effects of gradual depth variation and bottom friction on nonlinear long waves, including isolated solitons, periodic wave trains, and the leading solitary wave of an undular bore. A variable-coefficient weakly nonlinear model is used to represent shoaling, dispersive deformation, and frictional dissipation over slowly varying bathymetry. In the absence of friction, decreasing depth generally amplifies and narrows solitary waves, while increasing depth produces attenuation and broadening. Bottom friction counteracts shoaling-induced amplification, reduces wave speed, and causes cumulative phase delay and energy loss. Isolated solitons respond primarily through gradual changes in amplitude, width, and position, with stronger friction potentially generating a dispersive trailing tail. Periodic wave trains exhibit additional changes in wavelength, mean level, and spectral content because dissipation acts continuously and nonlinear interactions redistribute energy among successive crests. For an undular bore, the leading solitary wave undergoes the strongest bathymetric adjustment, but its evolution remains coupled to the trailing wavetrain; friction lowers the leading crest, weakens bore expansion, and suppresses secondary oscillations. The results show that bathymetric shoaling and bottom drag cannot, in general, be treated independently: their competition determines whether nonlinear amplification, dissipative decay, or dispersive restructuring dominates the observed wave field.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the main findings of research comparing the adiabatic evolution of an isolated solitary wave with the nonlocal evolution of an undular bore under variable topography and Chezy friction.
counterfactuals.output:
Research based on variable-coefficient KdV/Whitham theory found a fundamental difference between the two cases:

- **Isolated solitary wave:** Its parameters evolve adiabatically and essentially locally. Slow depth variation changes the balance between nonlinearity and dispersion, giving the familiar shoaling increase—without dissipation, the amplitude scales approximately as \(a\propto h^{-4/3}\) in the weakly nonlinear regime. Chezy drag adds cumulative amplitude decay and can offset or overwhelm shoaling. The pulse also changes width and speed and generally leaves a small shelf because its mass cannot remain exactly conserved while retaining a pure soliton shape.

- **Undular bore:** The leading wave cannot, in general, be treated as an isolated soliton obeying the same adiabatic law. Its amplitude and speed are selected by the modulation of the entire oscillatory bore, including the mean flow, wavenumber, trailing edge, upstream jump, and the bore’s previous passage over the bottom. Its evolution is therefore **nonlocal and history-dependent**.

- **Topography and friction act differently on a bore:** Shoaling modifies the whole modulation structure, not just the lead crest. Chezy friction changes the mean jump, damps the wavetrain—often especially the larger waves—and alters both edge trajectories and bore width. Thus local depth and a local friction coefficient alone are insufficient to predict the leading-wave amplitude.

- **Main practical conclusion:** Applying an isolated-solitary-wave shoaling/decay formula to the leading crest of an undular bore can produce substantial errors. The isolated wave can be modeled by an amplitude ODE, whereas the bore requires a Whitham-type modulation calculation, or an equivalent numerical treatment, over the full wave train. Only when the leading wave becomes effectively detached from the bore does isolated-soliton behavior become a reasonable approximation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a technical paper summary emphasizing that nonlinear interactions within an undular bore can cause additional leading-wave amplitude growth that traditional adiabatic solitary-wave theory cannot predict.
counterfactuals.output:
### Technical Paper Summary

This study examines the evolution of an undular bore propagating through a slowly varying environment, with particular attention to the growth of its leading wave. Traditional adiabatic solitary-wave theory treats the leading crest as an isolated soliton whose parameters adjust gradually in response to changes in depth, width, or background flow. Although this approach captures part of the shoaling response, it systematically underestimates the observed leading-wave amplitude.

The analysis shows that the leading crest remains dynamically coupled to the oscillatory wave train behind it. Nonlinear interactions within the bore transfer mass, momentum, and energy toward the front, producing additional amplitude growth beyond that caused by adiabatic deformation alone. Because isolated-solitary-wave theory neglects these collective bore-scale interactions, its conservation laws and amplitude–speed relations cannot account for this enhancement.

Numerical or asymptotic results demonstrate that the discrepancy becomes significant when the modulation of the bore and the environmental variation occur on comparable scales. The leading wave must therefore be modeled as part of a nonlinear, evolving wavetrain rather than as an independently adapting soliton. A full description requires a framework such as dispersive hydrodynamics, modulation theory, or direct simulation of the governing nonlinear dispersive equations.

The central conclusion is that leading-wave amplification in an undular bore is not solely an adiabatic shoaling effect. Internal nonlinear interactions provide an additional growth mechanism, making conventional solitary-wave predictions potentially non-conservative when estimating maximum crest heights and associated hazards.
